question: What are the three most architecturally significant differences between Neo4j Community Edition and the DozerDB fork/plugin, with authoritative citations? Cover: (1) the packaging model — full fork vs. bootstrapping plugin — and its consequences for upgrades and removal; (2) the license posture — GPLv3 vs. the Neo4j Enterprise commercial license — and what that implies for source availability and downstream redistribution; (3) the concrete feature deltas DozerDB restores from Enterprise (multi-database, enterprise constraints, backup/restore, high-limit store class) and which of those are re-implementations vs. re-enabled community-code paths.

ground_truth.authored_by: Perplexity Computer (analyst) with human review by rmholston420

canonical_facts.statement: DozerDB is a bootstrapping plugin that loads into an unmodified Neo4j Community Edition installation to enable enterprise-tier features, not a full source fork. This distinguishes it from ONgDB, which was a complete source fork of Neo4j Enterprise pre-3.5.

The plugin model means DozerDB can be added or removed at any time without recompiling or migrating Neo4j Community Edition; the underlying store format remains compatible with vanilla Community binaries when the plugin is uninstalled.

Neo4j Community Edition is licensed under GPLv3 and its source is publicly published; Neo4j Enterprise Edition is licensed under a commercial (proprietary) license and its source has not been published on GitHub since Neo4j 3.5 (November 2018).

DozerDB itself is GPLv3, matching the license of the Neo4j Community host it plugs into; this is a deliberate contrast with ONgDB's AGPLv3 posture, chosen by the DozerDB maintainer specifically to avoid AGPL's network-copyleft implications for downstream users.

DozerDB restores four enterprise-tier feature families onto Community Edition: (a) multi-database support (multiple named databases in one server, beyond the two — system + default — that Community allows); (b) enterprise-tier schema constraints (property-existence, property-type, and node/relationship key uniqueness constraints); (c) backup and restore (offline dump is in Community; DozerDB adds the online/hot-backup family that Community lacks); (d) advanced monitoring/diagnostics.

The DozerDB maintainer has explicitly stated that clustering, live/hot backups, and the high-limit store class are not primary DozerDB deliverables at the plugin layer; DozerDB's roadmap focuses on multi-database, composite/fabric-successor databases, enterprise metrics, and a modular ABAC-based security framework, with high-limit and live-backup features added only if the community demands them.

ground_truth.expected_answer_narrative: Neo4j Community Edition (GPLv3, source public) and Neo4j Enterprise Edition (commercial license, source no longer published since 3.5) diverge at three architecturally load-bearing levels. First, packaging: DozerDB is a GPLv3 bootstrapping plugin that loads into unmodified Neo4j Community binaries and can be added or removed at will; ONgDB by contrast attempted a full AGPLv3 fork of the Enterprise source tree and became legally and technically stalled. Second, license posture: because DozerDB is GPLv3 and Neo4j Community is GPLv3, redistribution and downstream modification are unambiguous; Enterprise remains proprietary and its source is not published, so any 'Enterprise features on Community' has to be a clean-room re-implementation or a re-enablement of Community-repo code paths, not a copy of Enterprise sources. Third, feature deltas: DozerDB restores multi-database support, enterprise schema constraints (property existence/type, node-key uniqueness), backup/restore, and monitoring/diagnostics. These are re-enabled or re-implemented against the GPLv3 Community codebase; clustering, live hot-backup, and the high-limit store class (1 quadrillion nodes) are explicitly not first-class DozerDB deliverables and remain Enterprise-exclusive or roadmap-conditional.
